opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this came up a lot for us when we were working on the time horizon work at METR. The basic setup is that we have a bunch of tasks, we've measured roughly how long each one takes a skilled human, and then for each model we look at whether it succeeds or fails on each task. We fit a logistic curve of success probability against the log of human task length, and the "time horizon" is just the point where that curve crosses fifty percent.

And you could obviously do something much fancier. You could add parameters for task domain, for how "messy" a task is, for whether it has an automatic scoring function, for the particular task family, and so on. Some of those almost certainly would improve the fit. Tasks really do vary in ways that aren't captured by human time alone.

But I think the way I think about it is: what is the model *for*? For us the main goal was a single, interpretable quantity that we could track across many models and over time, and ideally extrapolate. If you have a model with fifteen parameters, each new frontier model gives you a slightly different configuration, and it becomes really hard to say whether things are getting better, at what rate, and what that means. With one or two parameters per model, you can plot it and see a trend, and that trend turned out to be surprisingly clean, which is itself some evidence that the simple model is capturing something real.

There's also an overfitting concern that's quite concrete here. Our task suite isn't huge, maybe a couple hundred tasks, and the successes and failures are noisy. If you add a lot of flexibility you end up fitting idiosyncrasies of particular tasks rather than anything that generalizes. So I'd want any added complexity to earn its place: does it improve held-out prediction, not just in-sample fit?

That said, I don't think simplicity should be a cover for ignoring systematic misfit. One thing we did was check residuals: are there classes of tasks where the model is consistently over- or under-predicting success? Messier tasks, for example, tended to be harder than their length alone would suggest. When you see that kind of systematic pattern, it's telling you the one-dimensional story is incomplete, and you should at least report it, even if you keep the headline metric simple. So in practice my approach is: keep the primary model as simple as you can defend, be very upfront about where it fails, and do robustness checks showing the main conclusions, like the trend in time horizon, don't hinge on those simplifications.

r001.rationale: The response notes that tasks differ and discusses fit, simplicity, and overfitting, but it does not identify aggregation across potentially different task distributions as the reason the tradeoff is unclear.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we thought about a lot when we were trying to fit the curve for how AI task success relates to how long tasks take humans. The basic tension is that you can always get a better fit by adding parameters, but at some point you're just describing noise in your particular dataset rather than something real about the models.

The way I think about it is that the model should be as simple as the question you're actually trying to answer. For us, the question was something like, "Is there a single number that characterizes how capable a model is on these tasks, and does that number track with task length in a sensible way?" A logistic fit with a horizon parameter and a slope answers that question. If you need a bunch of extra terms to make the fit look good, that's often a sign that either the underlying variable isn't the right one, or your task suite has structure you haven't accounted for, like a cluster of tasks that are hard for reasons unrelated to length.

I also think it matters what you're going to do with the model. If the goal is forecasting, then a simpler model with worse in-sample fit often generalizes better, and you should be checking that by holding out tasks or holding out models rather than just staring at residuals on the data you fit on. If the goal is understanding, then sometimes the residuals are the interesting part. Where does the simple model fail? Those failures tell you about what else is going on.

And honestly, part of it is just being upfront about uncertainty. We tried to be clear that the fit is okay but not great, that there's a lot of variance across tasks at a given length, and that the specific numbers depend on choices like which tasks are in the suite and how you estimate human time. I'd rather report a simple model with honest error bars than a complicated model that looks precise but is overfit to a hundred and seventy tasks.

r001.rationale: The response notes that a task suite may contain clusters of tasks with different sources of difficulty, but it does not identify aggregation across potentially different task distributions as making the fit-versus-simplicity tradeoff unclear.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you want to use the model for. If you just want to summarize performance on tasks you’ve already measured, goodness of fit is pretty useful. But if you want to extrapolate to harder tasks or more capable systems, a better fit on the existing data doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve captured the right structure.

So I’d start with a simple model and ask where it fails. Are there systematic patterns in the residuals? Does adding complexity help predict held-out tasks, or does it just let you explain the observations you already have? Ideally, the extra complexity would also correspond to something you have an independent reason to expect matters for task success.

And I’d be wary of committing too strongly to one model. If several fairly simple models fit the data about equally well but make very different predictions, that’s an important uncertainty to preserve.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing a model based on its use, extrapolation, residuals, and held-out prediction, but does not identify aggregation across potentially different task distributions as a reason the fit-versus-simplicity tradeoff is unclear.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you want to use the model for. If you’re trying to summarize performance on tasks you’ve already measured, goodness of fit is pretty important. But if you’re trying to predict performance on substantially different tasks, or extrapolate to future systems, then fitting the existing data well isn’t enough. You need some reason to think the structure you’ve chosen will continue to apply.

Simplicity is useful there because it limits how much you can tailor the model to the particular observations you have. But I wouldn’t treat simplicity as an overriding objective, either. If a simple model systematically misses an important feature of task success, that’s a reason to make it more complicated.

So I’d want to compare a few plausible models, see how well they predict held-out observations, and check whether the conclusions I care about depend on which model I choose. If they do, I’d be more inclined to report that uncertainty than to say we’ve identified the right model.

r001.rationale: The response says the fit–simplicity balance depends on whether the goal is interpolation or extrapolation, but it does not identify aggregation across potentially different task distributions as the reason the trade-off is unclear.
